name: Lisbon
tagline: Seven hills, yellow trams and custard tarts by the Tagus
description:
Lisbon tumbles down seven hills to the broad, glittering Tagus, and every climb is rewarded with a miradouro, a lookout terrace where terracotta roofs, church domes and pastel façades spill toward the water. Yellow trams grind up impossibly steep lanes, laundry flaps between tiled buildings, and the smell of grilling sardines drifts from tiny tascas.

The city's layers tell a story of seafaring glory, earthquake and reinvention. The maze of Alfama survived the great 1755 quake and still feels like a village, while the grand Baixa was rebuilt afterward on a rational grid. Out in Belém, monuments of the Age of Discovery stand beside bakery queues for warm custard tarts, and across town former warehouses have become galleries, food halls and riverside bars.

Lisbon remains one of Western Europe's better-value capitals, and its pleasures are unhurried: a bica espresso at a marble counter, a cherry liqueur from a hole-in-the-wall bar, a mournful fado song in a candlelit room. Bring comfortable shoes with good grip and let the hills set the pace.

safety.notes: Lisbon is one of Europe's safest capitals, but pickpockets work tram 28, the Santa Justa Lift queue and crowded viewpoints. Politely ignore street sellers whispering offers of 'hashish' in the Baixa; it's usually bay leaves or worse.

tipping: Tipping is modest: leave small change at cafés and around 5–10% for good service at sit-down restaurants.
gettingAround: Lisbon's hills are steep, so mix walking with the metro, historic trams, funiculars and inexpensive ride-hailing. A reusable Navegante card loaded with credit works across the metro, buses, trams and river ferries.
tips: Wear shoes with real grip: the polished limestone calçada pavements are slippery even when dry and treacherous after rain.
Tram 28 is packed with tourists and pickpockets, so ride it early from the Martim Moniz terminus or take the quieter tram 12 or 24 for similar scenery.
Bread, olives and cheese placed on your table aren't free; you pay only for what you touch, so send them back if you don't want them.
Many museums and monuments close on Mondays, so plan Belém and the Tile Museum for other days.
The commuter ferry to Cacilhas costs a couple of dollars and delivers one of the best views of the Lisbon skyline.
Load a reusable Navegante card with pay-as-you-go credit for cheaper metro, bus, tram and ferry rides than single tickets.
etiquette: Portuguese is not Spanish, so say 'obrigado' (if you're male) or 'obrigada' (if you're female) rather than 'gracias'.
Stay completely silent during fado performances; chatting while a fadista sings is deeply disrespectful.
Greet shopkeepers with 'bom dia' in the morning and 'boa tarde' after noon.
Meals are leisurely, with lunch from about 13:00 and dinner rarely before 20:00.

neighborhoods.name: Alfama
neighborhoods.blurb: The city's oldest quarter, a maze of stairways, laundry lines, tiny squares and fado houses below the castle.

neighborhoods.name: Bairro Alto
neighborhoods.blurb: Sleepy by day, this hilltop grid of narrow streets turns into one big open-air bar after dark.

neighborhoods.name: Chiado
neighborhoods.blurb: Elegant and literary, with historic cafés, theaters, old bookshops and stylish boutiques.

neighborhoods.name: Belém
neighborhoods.blurb: The riverside home of Age of Discovery monuments, big museums and the city's most famous custard tarts.

neighborhoods.name: Príncipe Real
neighborhoods.blurb: A leafy, upscale enclave of concept stores, garden squares and some of the city's best restaurants.

dishes.name: Pastel de nata
dishes.description: Crisp, flaky pastry cups of caramelized egg custard, best eaten warm with a dusting of cinnamon.

dishes.name: Bacalhau à brás
dishes.description: Shredded salt cod scrambled with egg, onion and crisp matchstick potatoes, finished with black olives and parsley.

dishes.name: Sardinhas assadas
dishes.description: Fat sardines grilled over charcoal and served on bread, the smoky signature scent of Lisbon's June festivals.

dishes.name: Bifana
dishes.description: A soft roll stuffed with thin slices of pork marinated in garlic and white wine, often splashed with mustard or hot sauce.

dishes.name: Ginjinha
dishes.description: A sweet sour-cherry liqueur served in a tiny glass, sometimes with a boozy cherry, from hole-in-the-wall bars.

events.name: IndieLisboa
events.description: An adventurous international film festival screening independent features and shorts in cinemas across the city.

events.name: Festas de Lisboa
events.description: All June long, and above all on the night of June 12, the old quarters honor Saint Anthony with grilled sardines, street parties and parades.

events.name: NOS Alive
events.description: A major rock and pop festival on the riverside at Algés that draws international headliners for three summer nights.

events.name: Dia de São Martinho
events.description: On November 11, Lisbon celebrates St. Martin's Day with street-roasted chestnuts and the season's first young wine.

attractions.name: Belém Tower
attractions.description: This fairy-tale fortress rising from the Tagus once guarded the river approach and saw off the explorers of Portugal's Age of Discovery. Its stonework is carved with ropes, armillary spheres and even a rhinoceros, and the top terrace looks upriver to the great red suspension bridge.
attractions.bookingTip: The narrow spiral stair runs on a traffic-light system, so arrive at opening; a combined ticket with the Jerónimos Monastery saves money.

attractions.name: Jerónimos Monastery
attractions.description: A masterpiece of the flamboyant Manueline style, built with spice-trade riches and carved with twisting ropes, sea creatures and exotic plants. The two-story cloister is breathtaking, and Vasco da Gama's tomb lies in the church, which is free to enter.
attractions.bookingTip: Book the cloister online and go right at opening, then reward yourself with a warm custard tart from a nearby bakery.

attractions.name: Alfama
attractions.description: Lisbon's oldest quarter is a tangle of steep alleys, stairways and tiny squares that largely survived the 1755 earthquake. Get deliberately lost among laundry lines and tiled façades, catch the view from the Portas do Sol terrace, and stay for fado after dark.
attractions.hours: Always open; fado houses from about 20:00
attractions.bookingTip: Free to explore; book fado dinners ahead on weekends and wear shoes with good grip for the slippery paving.

attractions.name: São Jorge Castle
attractions.description: Crowning the highest hill of the old city, this Moorish-era castle has ramparts to walk, peacocks strutting through shady gardens and the finest panorama in Lisbon. Come in late afternoon to watch the sun set over the river and the red roofs of the Baixa.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy tickets online to skip the gate queue, and ride tram 12 or 28 up if the climb looks daunting.

attractions.name: Santa Justa Lift
attractions.description: A neo-Gothic iron elevator from 1902 that links the flat Baixa to the hilltop Chiado district. The ride is brief, but the lattice walkway at the top gives a superb view over the castle, Rossio square and the roofless ruins of the Carmo Convent.
attractions.bookingTip: Midday queues can reach an hour, so ride early or late, or walk to the upper platform from the Carmo side and pay just for the viewing deck.

attractions.name: Praça do Comércio
attractions.description: This vast riverside square, once the site of the royal palace destroyed in 1755, is framed by yellow arcades and a triumphal arch opening onto Rua Augusta. Walk through to the Cais das Colunas, where marble steps slip down into the Tagus, for a classic Lisbon sunset.
attractions.bookingTip: The square is free; pay a few dollars to ride up inside the Rua Augusta Arch for a rooftop view over it.

attractions.name: Mercado da Ribeira
attractions.description: Lisbon's main produce market has fed the city for more than a century; one hall still sells fish, fruit and flowers each morning, while the other is a buzzing food court of stalls run by well-known local chefs. Grab a spot at the communal tables and graze from bifanas to seafood rice.
attractions.hours: Food hall 10:00–00:00 daily; fresh market 06:00–14:00 Mon–Sat
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive before 12:30 or after 14:30 to find a seat, and browse the fresh-produce side early in the morning.

attractions.name: Calouste Gulbenkian Museum
attractions.description: An oil magnate's astonishingly rich private collection spans Egyptian antiquities, Persian carpets, Rembrandt and a dazzling room of René Lalique jewelry. The museum sits in a tranquil modernist garden of ponds, ducks and shady paths that is a joy in its own right.
attractions.bookingTip: Entry is free on Sunday afternoons, and the gardens are free every day and perfect for a picnic.

attractions.name: Lisbon Oceanarium
attractions.description: One of Europe's largest aquariums is built around a vast central tank where sharks, rays and a giant sunfish glide past as you circle it on two levels. Surrounding habitats recreate the coasts of four oceans, complete with sea otters, puffins and penguins.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy tickets online and arrive early on weekends, then ride the riverside cable car along the Parque das Nações waterfront.

attractions.name: National Tile Museum
attractions.description: Set in a 16th-century convent, this museum traces five centuries of Portugal's beloved azulejos, from Moorish geometric patterns to Art Deco. The showstopper is a long tiled panorama of Lisbon before the earthquake, and the gilded chapel is jaw-dropping.
attractions.bookingTip: It's a little outside the center, so take a bus from Praça do Comércio and plan lunch in the museum's tile-clad café.

hotels.name: Palácio Maré Alta
hotels.description: An 18th-century aristocrat's palace in Chiado, restored with painted ceilings, azulejo-lined corridors and a rooftop infinity pool gazing over the castle and the river. Spa treatments use Portuguese sea salt, and the bar pours rare old ports.

hotels.name: Casa do Fado Lento
hotels.description: Twelve rooms in a tile-fronted Alfama townhouse, decorated with vintage guitars, handwoven rugs and small balconies over a stepped alley. The owner hosts intimate fado evenings in the stone-vaulted lounge twice a week.

hotels.name: Hostel Sardinha Feliz
hotels.description: A bright, beach-themed hostel above the Cais do Sodré nightlife strip, with capsule-style bunks, a rooftop terrace and nightly family dinners. Trains to the Cascais beaches leave from the station across the road.

hotels.name: Hotel Cortiça Belém
hotels.description: Cork paneling, pale oak and river-blue textiles give this riverside design hotel a calm, contemporary feel rooted in Portugal's maritime heritage. There's an outdoor pool in the garden and bikes for the flat riverside path to the Tower.

hotels.name: Casa Nobre das Muralhas
hotels.description: Built against the medieval walls of the castle hill, this noble house keeps its stone arches, a tiled chapel and a terrace garden with one of the best breakfast views in Lisbon. Nights are blissfully quiet, since the castle quarter empties after dark.

hotels.name: Estúdios Lilás
hotels.description: Modern studios and one-bedroom apartments on a jacaranda-lined avenue, each with a kitchenette and a small balcony. The metro, the Gulbenkian gardens and a neighborhood market are all a few minutes' walk away.

restaurants.name: Salmoura
restaurants.description: Behind an unmarked door just off the great square, a young chef reinvents Portuguese staples like salt cod, cozido and cataplana as delicate tasting courses. The wine pairings unearth tiny producers from the Douro, Dão and Alentejo.
restaurants.signatureDish: Salt cod confit with chickpea cream

restaurants.name: Tasca da Dona Arminda
restaurants.description: A six-table tasca where the owner has been charring sardines on a charcoal grill in the street outside for decades. Order the day's fish, a tomato salad and a jug of house wine, and expect a bill so small it looks like a mistake.

restaurants.name: Confeitaria Rio Seco
restaurants.description: Custard tarts leave the oven every twenty minutes at this tiled pastry shop near the monastery, their tops scorched and their pastry shattering. Dust them with cinnamon and powdered sugar and eat them warm with a bica.

restaurants.name: Cervejaria Polvo Largo
restaurants.description: A cavernous, clattering seafood hall with river views, where clams in garlic and coriander, tiger prawns and whole crabs are sold by weight. Finish the Lisbon way with a prego steak sandwich instead of dessert.

restaurants.name: Petisqueira Cais Torto
restaurants.description: A narrow bar near the market serving petiscos, Portugal's answer to tapas, such as octopus salad, braised pork cheeks and cheese-stuffed peppers. It's a lively warm-up stop before the bars of Pink Street.

restaurants.name: Casa Goa Xacuti
restaurants.description: Lisbon's long ties with Goa shine at this family-run spot, where curries fragrant with coconut, tamarind and roasted spices come with rice and puffy bread. Don't miss the pork vindaloo, a Portuguese garlic-and-wine dish transformed in India and brought home again.
restaurants.signatureDish: Chicken xacuti with coconut and roasted spices

restaurants.name: Casa de Fado Candeia
restaurants.description: Candles, stone walls and a dozen tables set the scene for nightly fado, sung by rotating local fadistas between courses of hearty Portuguese cooking. Silence falls when the guitars begin, so save your chatter for between sets.

restaurants.name: Taberna Calçada Alta
restaurants.description: Wooden tables, a blackboard of daily specials and hams hanging over the bar define this friendly taberna halfway up the hill to Chiado. The bacalhau à brás, creamy with egg and crisp potato straws, is a local benchmark.

experiences.name: Vento Norte Sunset Sail on the Tagus
experiences.description: Sail from the Belém docks on a classic yacht as the sun sinks behind the great suspension bridge, gliding past the Tower, the Discoveries Monument and the Cristo Rei statue. The skipper swaps sailing stories while you sip chilled vinho verde.

experiences.name: Nata Masterclass by the River
experiences.description: Learn the secrets of Portugal's favorite pastry in a working bakery near the market, from rolling the spiral-laminated dough to cooking the lemon-scented custard. You'll eat your warm tarts with coffee and take the recipe home.

experiences.name: Alfama Fado and Petiscos Night Walk
experiences.description: Wander Alfama's lamplit alleys with a local guide, sampling ginjinha, cured meats and flame-grilled chouriço at neighborhood tascas. The night ends in a tiny fado house where amateur singers take turns by candlelight.

experiences.name: Sintra Palaces and Cabo da Roca Day Trip
experiences.description: Meet in the grand riverside square for a day in the fairy-tale hills of Sintra, touring the candy-colored Pena Palace and the mystical gardens of Quinta da Regaleira. The afternoon swings out to the windswept cliffs of Cabo da Roca, the westernmost point of mainland Europe.
